analysis.investment_thesis: Devyani's franchise QSR model — KFC, Pizza Hut, Costa Coffee — rides India's eating-out boom with 19.3% revenue CAGR, but debt-funded expansion has pushed D/E to 1.71 and finance costs to ₹267 Cr, wiping out net profits in FY24 and FY25. At ₹13,279 Cr market cap and 127x forward P/E on a loss-making business, there is zero margin of safety.
key_strengths: Promoter holding of 61.37% (RJ Corp) provides strong alignment and execution backing from a proven consumer-business family group.
Operating cash flow of ₹900 Cr in FY25 (5/5 years positive OCF) shows the underlying unit economics work at restaurant level despite P&L losses.
India's QSR penetration is <5% vs China's 15%+ — genuinely large TAM with secular urbanisation tailwind; Devyani is among India's top 3 QSR operators.
key_risks: D/E of 1.71 (borrowings ₹3,343 Cr in FY25, up from ₹1,254 Cr in FY22) — 3x Kedia's 0.4 hard limit; franchise expansion is essentially levered at high cost.
Net profit has been loss-making in 7 of last 9 years — business cannot convert EBITDA growth (29.4% 9Y CAGR) to PAT due to Ind AS 116 lease costs and finance charges.
Franchise model means royalty payments to Yum! Brands structurally cap margins; no IP ownership, no pricing leverage — pure execution arbitrage.
red_flags: Market cap ₹13,279 Cr with forward P/E of 127x on a loss-making company — paying decade-ahead growth today with zero earnings cushion.
D/E of 1.71 — among the worst in this comparison set; borrowings nearly doubled from ₹1,565 Cr (FY23) to ₹3,343 Cr (FY25) in just 2 years.
Negative net worth history (₹-189 Cr equity in FY20) and persistent losses — balance sheet quality has only recovered post-IPO equity infusion.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Devyani operates in a genuinely attractive sector — India's QSR market is underpenetrated and growing at 15–20% annually. Revenue growing from ₹1,012 Cr (FY16) to ₹4,951 Cr (FY25), EBITDA CAGR of 29.4%, and consistently positive OCF suggest the store-level model works. Promoter at 61.37% and RJ Corp's strong consumer-sector track record are positives Kedia would appreciate. But the capital structure is broken: ₹267 Cr in annual finance costs on a company earning ₹853 Cr EBITDA leaves almost nothing for equity holders after depreciation (also massively inflated by Ind AS 116 lease capitalisation).

The expansion into Thailand, Nigeria, and Nepal shows large aspirations — but each market requires capital without guaranteed returns. At ₹13,279 Cr market cap and 127x forward P/E, the market has priced a perfect long-term execution with no room for a single year of store underperformance, rent spike, or macro slowdown. For Kedia, this is a sector he'd want exposure to — but at 200–500 Cr market cap in an early-stage franchisee. Devyani today is a fully-valued mid-cap, not a discovery opportunity.
